Note: Aelius Aristides and Artemidorus provide two unusually rich Roman-period Greek approaches to dreams. Aristides presents dreams, especially those associated with Asclepius, within an autobiographical religious and therapeutic narrative, while Artemidorus systematizes dream interpretation as a technical practice sensitive to the dreamer’s social position, occupation, circumstances, and experience.

Oribasius and Libanius were both closely connected with Emperor Julian. Oribasius served as Julian’s physician and compiled the Medical Collections at his request, while Libanius became one of Julian’s major literary supporters and commemorators. The works therefore belong to the same late-fourth-century intellectual and imperial network.

Libanius and Gregory present sharply opposed rhetorical interpretations of Emperor Julian. Libanius praises and defends Julian and his religious program, whereas Gregory’s Invectives Against Julian attack the emperor’s religious and cultural policies. Together the corpora preserve competing pagan and Christian constructions of the same ruler and the struggle over Hellenic and Christian identity.
